Not all beaches are equal. The water clarity, the property access, the week you travel, the room category within the resort — these are the decisions that separate a genuinely remarkable trip from a good one.

Why Beach Travel

Not All Beaches
Are Worth the Flight

A week in Grace Bay looks nothing like a week in Cancún, even though both are sold as "Caribbean beach." One has water so clear you can see the seafloor from a hundred yards out. The other has an open bar and a swim-up pool. Both are valid — but only one is what most people are actually picturing when they book.

The details that separate a great beach property from an average one are rarely in the listing. Which rooms have unobstructed water views? Which has direct beach access vs. a shared stretch fifty meters from the resort? Is the snorkeling actually good from the property, or do you need a boat? Which months mean flat water, and which months mean two-foot chop that turns your horizon view into white noise?

We've stayed at enough overwater villas, private-island resorts, and boutique beach properties to know where the gap is — between what the brochure promises and what a week there actually delivers. That gap is what we're paid to close.

Where to Go

Six Destinations We Know in Detail

Each delivers a different version of beach travel. The right one depends on what you're actually after — and when you can go.

Destination Photography · Maldives
Indian Ocean
Maldives
The benchmark for overwater living. Each resort occupies its own private atoll — no shared beaches, no crowds. House reef snorkeling directly off your villa, some of the clearest water on earth, and a calendar that rewards the right booking window. Best November through April.
Overwater Villas House Reef Private Atoll
Destination Photography · Turks & Caicos
Caribbean
Turks & Caicos
Grace Bay consistently ranks among the top beaches on earth — and it earns it. Shallow turquoise water, powder sand, and a small collection of genuinely excellent resort properties. The ideal Caribbean choice for those who take water quality seriously.
Grace BayProvidenciales
Destination Photography · Seychelles
Indian Ocean
Seychelles
Granite boulders, tropical forest, and beaches that feel like they were designed. Spread across 115 islands — the journey between them is part of the experience. Best combined as a multi-island itinerary. November through April for calmer water.
MahéPraslinLa Digue
Destination Photography · St. Barth's
Caribbean
St. Barth's
Small, unhurried, and deliberately refined. No mega-resorts, no cruise ships — just a collection of boutique hotels and private villas, exceptional dining, and twelve beaches worth exploring. The Caribbean at its most understated.
GustaviaVilla StaysBoutique
Destination Photography · South Pacific
South Pacific
Bora Bora & French Polynesia
Overwater bungalows invented here. The lagoon around Bora Bora is a spectacle in itself — shallow, warm, impossibly colored. Remote in the most satisfying way. Best May through October when trade winds keep conditions ideal.
Bora BoraMooreaOverwater
Destination Photography · Caribbean
Eastern Caribbean
St. Lucia & Anguilla
Two Caribbean islands with completely different personalities — St. Lucia for lush drama and Piton-framed beaches, Anguilla for flat water, boutique quiet, and some of the best shoreline dining in the region. Often combined with a night in Antigua.
St. LuciaAnguillaCombination

When to Go

Beach Season by Destination

Caribbean Peak
December – April
The definitive window for Caribbean and Turks & Caicos travel. Low humidity, consistent sun, and the flattest water of the year. Rates and demand peak accordingly — book four to six months out.
Best for Caribbean
Indian Ocean Window
November – April
The primary season for Maldives and Seychelles. Calm lagoons, excellent visibility, and reliable sunshine. The shoulder edges of this window (November and April) offer comparable conditions at lower occupancy.
South Pacific Season
May – October
The dry season for Bora Bora and French Polynesia. Trade winds keep conditions ideal — cool breezes, clear water, and the dramatic Bora Bora lagoon at its most vivid. Avoid peak European summer for fewer crowds.

A Note from Mark

On Beach Travel

Mark Sole
Founder & Travel Director · Hit Your Mark Travel

"The most common beach travel mistake isn't choosing the wrong destination — it's choosing the right destination in the wrong month, or the right resort but the wrong room category, or a property that looks perfect in photos and has a shared beach that's shoulder-to-shoulder in peak season. I've been to enough of these places to know that a beach trip either delivers the feeling people are after or it doesn't, and the difference is almost always in the details that didn't make the listing. That's the work worth doing before you book — and it's the work we do for every trip."

Common Questions

Beach & Island Escapes — FAQ

Questions we hear most when planning beach and island travel. More detail on the full FAQ page.

How do I choose between the Maldives, Caribbean, and South Pacific?+
Each delivers something different. The Maldives is unmatched for overwater villa luxury and marine life, but is primarily a resort experience with limited cultural exploration. The Caribbean combines beach access with island character, food culture, and excursion options. The South Pacific — Fiji, Bora Bora, Cook Islands — blends extraordinary natural scenery with genuinely warm hospitality. The right choice depends on how far you want to travel and what kind of experience you're looking for.
What should I look for in a luxury beach resort?+
Beyond the obvious — beach quality, water clarity, room category — the variables that separate good resorts from great ones are service culture, food quality, how crowded the beach actually gets, and whether the property genuinely delivers on what its marketing promises. I visit properties personally before recommending them, so my suggestions are based on real experience.
What's the best time of year for beach travel?+
Entirely destination-dependent. The Caribbean's high season runs December–April, avoiding hurricane season (June–November). The Maldives is excellent November–April in the dry season. Southeast Asia's beach destinations follow different monsoon patterns by coast. I plan timing specifically to avoid peak costs without compromising conditions.
Are all-inclusive resorts worth considering for beach trips?+
In the right context, yes. A well-run all-inclusive removes the friction of per-meal billing and budgeting, and the best ones deliver genuine quality. The mistake is treating "all-inclusive" as a blanket category. The experience at a $200/night property and a $600/night property are fundamentally different, and I advise accordingly.
Can I combine multiple islands in a single trip?+
Yes, and often worth doing. A Caribbean trip might pair one quiet resort island with one more active island. A South Pacific trip might combine Bora Bora with Moorea or the Cook Islands. I design multi-island itineraries around how each destination complements the others — in terms of pace, character, and what you want to do each day.
How far in advance should I book a beach resort?+
For peak season travel — Christmas, February, spring break — 6–12 months in advance is standard for the best properties. Shoulder season allows more flexibility, sometimes 3–4 months. Top Maldives properties and certain Caribbean Christmas-period dates can book 12+ months out. The best rooms go first.
What's the difference between a beach resort with and without a house reef?+
A house reef — a coral reef directly accessible by swimming or snorkeling from the beach — is one of the most valuable features for guests who want marine life access without a boat. In the Maldives especially, house reef quality varies significantly by atoll and property age. I factor reef condition into property recommendations for any client who plans to snorkel or dive.
Do I need to be a strong swimmer to enjoy a beach resort trip?+
No. Overwater villas, poolside relaxation, and shore-based activities are all fully accessible without swimming. Snorkeling with a life vest is available at virtually every beach resort. If swimming is a concern, I select properties with calm, shallow lagoons rather than open ocean exposure.
